body.text: Tomorrow night election watchers will witness Victorians delivering such a pounding to their twelve-year-old Labor government that it will leave the party with its lowest share of Legislative Assembly seats in at least thirty years and probably much longer. Adding colour and movement will be the height from which the fall begins: the Andrews government’s spectacular 2022 victory that delivered Labor its second-biggest Legislative Assembly seat haul in the state’s history. (The biggest was under Steve Bracks in 2002.)
Australian governments going from landslide victory to landslide loss are unusual. Western Australia in 2018 probably qualifies, but this shift will be bigger.

The last time the state administered a big defeat to the ALP was in 1996, when the Kennett government was re-elected with 53.5 per cent of the two-party-preferred vote. But that’s a proverbial foreign country now — people lived, behaved, thought and voted differently then — and those voters are a minority of today’s roll. This one will be larger, and the huge swing, massive in some places, will throw up unprecedented results in parts of the state.

I write “swing” in the singular but of course that no longer covers it. In particular, there’s now a much more formidable One Nation. The fundamental electoral change across the country this century has been the erosion of major-party loyalty and the decline in their support, which over the past eighteen months has been turbocharged by One Nation’s drawing of support from the pollsters’ “others” and from the major parties.

At time of writing the polls all agree the government is headed for a calamity and the Coalition will get the most lower house seats. But One Nation’s polled primary vote is all over the place. Resolve in Nine’s papers, taken from last Friday to Sunday night, has the party on 25 per cent. Newspoll in the Australian, surveyed Friday to Wednesday evening, reckons it’s only 18. Redbridge in the Fin, perhaps a bit outdated at 13–20 November, has 23. But DemosAU, from Saturday to Wednesday, says just 16.

These dates matter more than before because of the increasing proportion of early voters. As Antony Green’s rolling tabulation shows, by the end of Wednesday 35 per cent of the electoral roll had cast a vote. Another 15 per cent have applied for postal votes, of which around 11 or 12 per cent will use them. Assuming around 90 per cent eventual turnout, and even allowing for votes popped in the mail from Thursday to election day, it’s likely that around half of eventual turnout had made their choice by the end of Wednesday. So a big chunk of survey respondents were answering a question about something they’ve already done. In theory, late polls should therefore be getting more accurate. In practice, so far, it’s not clear they are. (The electoral commission said it anticipates around 60 per cent of voters will have done the deed before Saturday, and the numbers so far back that up.)

For the others, surveys have the Coalition on 31–35 per cent, Labor 19–23 and Greens 13–17. DemosAU and Newspoll, which both polled until Wednesday, are at the upper end for the Greens. Two-party-preferred estimates start at around 55 per cent for the Coalition versus Labor and peak at 59. A couple of polls have surprisingly registered greater-than-asterisk support for the Victorian Socialists, which would matter in a little terms of preferences to the Greens and Labor.

One Nation won its first Legislative Council seat in 2022 and will certainly take several this time, very likely offering a one-stop shop for the new government to reach a majority to pass legislation. The Greens will probably provide another route (and Labor too, of course).
And the lower house? Well, pick a number.

At any election, support for each party is geographically diverse. If this was not the case (if it was totally uniform) at a single-member electorate contest (like all Australia’s lower house contests outside the ACT and Tasmania) the party with the biggest overall vote would win 100 per cent of seats. One Nation generally gets more spread than most: in particular its vote roughly increases the further away you get from a capital city’s CBD. Ideally, a party wants to maximise that lumpiness — but not beyond the point where it’s wasting lots of support in safe seats. So if One Nation receives, say, 20 per cent overall, it’ll want it to max out in some electorates in the low 40s or more.

Preferences are of course also extremely important. Partly because of how-to-vote cards, around 65 to 70 per cent of voters who put a “1” next to Labor will then number the Coalition ahead of One Nation. A similar percentage of Coalition “1” voters will place One Nation ahead of Labor. When a party makes it to the final round, its preferences aren’t distributed. The upshot is that One Nation would much rather face Labor than the Coalition in a final two-candidate-preferred count so it can reap all those Coalition preferences.

But Labor is going to do very badly, particularly in rural areas where it’s likely to drop out in the second-last (“three-candidate-preferred”) count in most of them. So its accumulated preferences will be distributed mostly to the Coalition against One Nation.

By “accumulated” I mean including preferences from candidates who have already been eliminated. In Labor’s case the accumulation will mostly have come from the Greens, whose voters are even more anti–One Nation than Labor’s.
So to win in rural areas One Nation will need very big primary votes.

One Nation’s other route is via formerly strong Labor territory where it can face the ALP in the final count and receive buckets of Coalition preferences. Two-candidate-preferred counts against Labor are most likely in outer-suburban, low-income, hitherto-traditional Labor seats. Antony (him again, officially retired but not idle) has mapped out 2025 federal One Nation votes onto Victorian boundaries. (One Nation only ran in a handful of seats in the 2022 state election, so we can’t use those.) The darker brown indicates high One Nation support in May 2025. In the second map, showing Melbourne, hovering your cursor over each seat shows votes, and the ones with large Labor margins are the ones that present possibilities. They include, for example, Lara in the west of the metropolitan map, though not so much Bass in the southeast because Liberal preferences are more likely to be distributed in the former.

One Nation’s support has roughly tripled since May 2025, and we can’t assume all the new voters are similar to the ones who were doing it before it was cool. In fact they’re probably rather different. This means that 2025 results are only a vague indicator of likely relative support. I’ll also be watching lighter brown, safe Labor seats in the north that swung strongly against the government four years ago, such as Mill Park, Yan Yean (part of whose swing can be attributed to a retiring member) and Thomastown.

The Greens are polling so well by historical standards that their primary vote as a proportion of Labor’s looks like being the biggest-ever seen nationally, certainly outside Tasmania. (In Newspoll it’s 85 per cent!) Their voters’ preferences will help Labor survive in some seats, but the minor party will beat the major one into the two-candidate-preferred count against the Liberal in lots of others.

The Greens will get a big percentage of ALP preferences, but from measly Labor support, and there will be swings to the Liberals in just the kind of seats the Greens are competitive in. That’s because the first-preference swing to the Coalition will be small to negligible statewide but large and against it in rural seats with big One Nation votes, and in the Coalition’s favour where One Nation doesn’t do very well. (Competitive seats for the Greens tend to sit in the latter category.)

For this reason, and in the absence of a sitting MP’s personal vote, regaining Prahran (narrowly lost to the Libs in a by-election last year) will be a big challenge. Yes, they’ll have the benefit of Labor’s how-to-vote cards (absent in the by-election) but that source of preferences will be much depleted and the Liberal primary vote bigger than 2022.

More Liberal primary votes also means more voters influenced by how-to-vote cards favouring Labor over the Greens. (They will also be praying for no repeat of last year’s federal election: then, their overall vote stood still but contained swings to them in uncompetitive electorates, and against them where it mattered, most famously in the leader’s electorate.)

The Greens will also be hoping for decent primary vote swings to get one or two of Footscray, Northcote, Pascoe Vale and Preston. And it’s difficult to see the Greens losing the three they hold: Brunswick (also sans a sitting MP, but on a big 13.5 per cent margin), Melbourne and Richmond. All three margins are robust and — importantly — against the ALP, and polls suggest a statewide rise in Greens support.

So beneath the mayhem, what can we expect tomorrow night, or at least when counting is over? One close-to-sure thing is a Coalition majority. Greens on three or four (most observers are expecting more than I am). One Nation: anything from zero to ten; and a few independents. Labor’s haul, as with the Coalition’s, depends partly on One Nation’s.
Let’s say Coalition on between fifty-two and fifty-seven and Labor between eighteen and twenty-three. •
